question: Why do hospitals nowadays rarely give whole blood to patients?

options.A: Whole blood carries no oxygen-carrying capacity
options.B: Patients usually only need specific blood components
options.C: Whole blood spoils within two hours of collection
options.D: Processing whole blood is too expensive for hospitals

explanation: Great job thinking like a clinician! Blood is separated into parts so patients get precisely what they lack—like just red cells or platelets—rather than getting components they don't need. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h1)

question: Why is double-checking the patient's ID band considered the absolute most important rule before a blood transfusion?

options.A: It ensures the hospital billing department charges the correct patient
options.B: It guarantees the blood donor receives proper compensation
options.C: It prevents clerical errors that can cause fatal incompatible reactions
options.D: It speeds up the time it takes to deliver blood from the lab

explanation: Spotting identity mistakes saves lives! Giving blood to the wrong person is a major cause of dangerous reactions, making this check vital. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which blood type is known as the universal red cell donor because almost anyone can safely receive it in emergencies?
explanation: You've got this! Type O negative red cells have no main antigens, so they won't trigger an attack in most recipients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the main reason lab scientists perform a crossmatch before releasing blood?

options.A: To check for hidden antibodies and ensure true compatibility between donor and recipient
options.B: To determine the patient's exact height and weight for dosage calculations
options.C: To sterilize the blood product before it leaves the blood bank
options.D: To measure the exact volume of red blood cells in the donor bag

explanation: Crossmatching is like a test-drive in a test tube! It mixes donor cells with patient serum to catch any immune clashes early. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h2)

question: When should you take a patient's baseline vital signs when getting ready to give a blood transfusion?

options.B: Only when the patient complains of fever
options.C: Six hours after the transfusion finishes
options.D: The evening before the procedure is scheduled

explanation: Taking vitals right before the infusion gives you a clear starting point so you can easily spot if anything changes later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h3)

question: How many nurses must check the blood bag details against the patient's ID band?

options.D: A nurse and a laboratory technician

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are better than one! Having two qualified nurses check together is a mandatory safety net. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h3)

question: Which IV fluid is the ONLY one safe to use alongside blood products?
explanation: Normal saline is isotonic and friendly to red blood cells, preventing them from bursting or clumping like other fluids might. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h4)

question: Why do nurses prefer using a large-bore cannula (like an 18-gauge) for blood transfusions?

options.A: It prevents the physical damage and destruction of red blood cells
options.B: It prevents the IV site from swelling or leaking into the tissues
options.C: It allows the nurse to infuse multiple medications at the same time
options.D: It reduces the need to check vital signs during the first fifteen minutes

explanation: Think of it like a wide pipe versus a tiny straw—narrow needles can squeeze and break fragile red blood cells, causing damage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h4)

question: How fast should you run a blood transfusion during the very first fifteen minutes?

options.A: As fast as the gravity pump can squeeze
options.B: Completely shut off until vitals stabilize
options.D: Slowly, around 50 to 60 drops per minute

explanation: Starting slow is a smart safety habit! If a reaction starts, a slow rate means less bad blood enters the body before you catch it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h5)

question: Within how many hours must a single unit of packed red blood cells be completely infused?
explanation: Keep an eye on the clock! Blood must finish within four hours so bacteria don't start multiplying in room temperature. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h5)

question: When is the best time to check the second set of vital signs after starting a blood transfusion?

options.B: At the very end of the bag

explanation: The 15-minute mark is crucial because most serious acute reactions happen right at the beginning of the infusion. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h6)

question: Your patient suddenly complains of lower back pain and chills mid-transfusion. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Ignore the symptoms unless the blood pressure drops significantly
options.B: Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the vein open with saline
options.C: Leave the room quickly to fetch the attending physician
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down and give prescribed paracetamol

explanation: Trust your instincts! Back pain and chills are classic warning signs of a hemolytic reaction—stop the infusion right away. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which symptom strongly points to an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
explanation: When red cells break down inside the body, the kidneys take a hit, which often shows up as sharp lower back or flank pain. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h7)

question: What usually causes Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)?

options.A: A mismatched ABO blood type between donor and recipient
options.B: Bacterial contamination of the red blood cells during storage
options.C: An allergic response to donor plasma proteins in the blood bag
options.D: Infusing blood too rapidly for the patient's cardiovascular system to handle

explanation: TACO happens when fluid goes in faster than a patient's heart can pump it, causing fluid backup in the lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h7)

question: What fluid should you use to flush the IV tubing after a blood transfusion is complete?
explanation: A normal saline flush nicely clears out any remaining blood products from the line without harming the patient's cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h8)

question: Which of these details is NOT necessary to write down in your notes after a blood transfusion?

options.A: The name of the blood donor's family members
options.B: The product serial number and volume given
options.C: The start and stop times of the infusion

explanation: Donor privacy is key! Blood banks keep donor details strictly confidential, so they never appear in your patient's chart. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h8)
